That larger payment will also be earmarked for underfunded city pensions.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: The City Council's Latino Caucus united in opposition to Stonepeak because of the company’s 2025 acquisition of Omni Air International, which has provided long-haul deportation flights for the Department of Homeland Security. entries.title: NBA 2K27 Review: The latest version brings you back to the playground
entries.summary: <p>The distance between “highly recruited high school basketball star with the world at your fingertips” and “couch surfing at your cousin’s run-down Brooklyn apartment” is inches, not miles.</p><p>That’s Lesson No. 1 in “NBA 2K27” as the “2K” franchise continues to sit near the top of the sports gaming mountain with its 28th annual installment, released Sept. 4 for Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S and Windows.</p><p>As usual, the focus of the game starts and ends with the MyPlayer/MyCareer modes, in which you choose a build path and start a story-line that feels like a movie mashup of “He Got Game” and “White Men Can’t Jump.”</p><p>You’re still playing as “MP,” the default name used for the cinematic cuts in the single-game storyline (and yes, that’s for a female character as well). You’re also still facing real-life obstacles in pursuit of stardom. Without spoiling the plot, “MP” starts off as a standout high school player, throwing you right into a game to show off your skills. It’s hard not to drop 30 points on the competition, which is the purpose here.</p><p>After that dominance, a booster hands you the keys to his $200,000 sports car and, just like that, life changes. No full ride to Duke, no instant stardom. Instead, it’s a fast-forward to two years after your car accident, when you’re lying around on your free-loading cousin Cam’s musty couch, trying to refocus on your dream of making the NBA with New York’s famous playground Rucker Park as the launching point.</p><p>Succeed there and you get a G-League contract. Slay the G-League and you get drafted to the NBA. That best sums up the “Fire & Concrete” storyline as you also build your player up for “The City,” the online-only environment introduced in “NBA 2K21.”</p><p>Warning: As with previous “2K” installments, beware of the microtransactions, in which Virtual Currency — purchased with real money — can be used to advance characters more quickly. Even if you’re successful in the storyline, your player will have an 80ish overall ranking out of a possible 97. For this review, there were already gamers playing online with rankings in the mid-to-high 90s — while trash-talking, of course — because they spent real cash on boosts and talents.</p><p>One great addition is a MyPlayer mode in which you can drop your player into five historical eras: Magic vs. Bird (1984), Michael Jordan (1991), Kobe (2003), LeBron (2010) and Steph Curry (2016). What’s great about these eras is how authentic they look and feels. Start off in ’84 and the locker rooms, broadcast styles and scoreboards match the looks and sounds of the ’80s.</p><p>That’s why “NBA 2K” always works — the details. They show up again in the other popular mode, MyNBA, in which you have full general-manager control over your NBA or WNBA front office, trades, the draft and the fortunes of your organization.</p><p>However, watch out, Bulls fans: Rookie forward Caleb Wilson plays better than his disrespectful 77 ranking, especially on defense, but the Bulls don’t have a great roster overall. You’ll spend a good amount of time looking for trades.</p><p>As for the gameplay itself, serious changes were made on defense. They’re an improvement but need a tweaking.</p><p>Has “NBA 2K27” made wholesale changes overall? No. It feels more like subtle tinkering that still moves the series forward. That’s why it gets a solid B-plus.</p><p>Either way, “2K” remains the standard, Cam’s stinky couch and all.</p>

entries.title: Pregnant girl, 16, loses baby, may not walk again after classmate shoots her in Little Village, prosecutors say
entries.summary: <p>A pregnant 16-year-old lost her baby and may not walk again after a 17-year-old classmate allegedly shot her in the back after harassing her earlier this month in Little Village, Cook County prosecutors said. </p><p>Angel David Funez-Reyes, 17, was charged with felony aggravated battery and misdemeanor unlawful use of a weapon, according to Chicago police in a statement and a spokesperson for the Cook County state's attorney's office. Police earlier indicated he was charged as a juvenile.</p><p>A judge ordered Funez-Reyes detained while awaiting trial at the Leighton Criminal Court building during a Tuesday detention hearing. </p><p>Prosecutors say Funez-Reyes had been allegedly harassing the girl for weeks in a class they shared at school, asking her about gang affiliation.</p><p>Funez-Reyes is also alleged to have flashed a gun at the girl and her boyfriend six hours before the shooting, according to prosecutors. </p><p>When she and another girl later saw Funez-Reyes around 7:11 p.m. Sept. 7 in the 2200 block of South Sawyer Avenue, an argument ensued. It was then that she began asking about a gun he had concealed in a hooded sweatshirt. </p><p>As the victim turned to walk away, Funez-Reyes allegedly shot her once in the back before fleeing in a black vehicle that was stationed nearby, prosecutors said. The girl was taken in serious condition to Mount Sinai Hospital for treatment.</p><p>Prosecutors said the girl likely will not walk again and lost the pregnancy as a result of her injuries.</p><p>Funez-Reyes also faces vehicular hijacking charges. Prosecutors indicated he was released from electronic monitoring Aug. 18 and was placed under a 9 p.m. curfew. </p><p>Funez-Reyes had been arrested two days before the shooting for aggravated assault, unlawful use of a weapon, possession of ammunition, and obstructing identification after he allegedly threatened people with a utility knife while shouting gang-related epithets, according to prosecutors. </p><p>Prosecutors claimed he lied to police about his identity during the arrest, when two rounds of live ammunition and the knife were found on him<b>. </b>Funez-Reyes will appear in court on those charges on Sept. 25.</p><p>Funez-Reyes is due back on court on Oct. 7 on the shooting of the girl, officials said. <br></p>

entries.title: Man stabbed, critically wounded on West Side
entries.summary: <p>Police are looking for the assailant responsible for slicing the neck of a man Wednesday morning, critically injuring him during an argument in the city's Austin neighborhood. </p><p>The man, 51, was outside in the 100 block of South Mason Avenue around 7:50 a.m. when he was approached by someone he knew and an argument started, Chicago police said. </p><p>The man was stabbed in the neck and was taken to Mount Sinai Hospital, where he was in critical condition, police said. </p><p>Area 4 detectives were investigating. </p>

entries.title: Ravinia will kick off $38 million more in renovations, this time to 122-year-old Martin Theatre
entries.summary: <p>Ravinia Festival announced another series of renovations on Wednesday, this time to the Martin Theatre, the last original structure standing from when the 36-acre wooded park in Highland Park opened in 1904.</p><p>The Martin Theatre refresh will cost an estimated $38 million. The Northbrook-based Negaunee Foundation gifted Ravinia the funds to complete the modernization project.</p><p>The building will close down after English singer-songwriter Jacob Collier performs on Sept. 23, and the first phase of construction will begin on the Martin in October, according to a press release. Next summer, the renovations will pause for performances slated during the 2027 season, but work will resume shortly after it ends, then officially reopen to the public during the 2028 season.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-6f0000" name="image-6f0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7f8efa7/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5400x3031+0+310/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbf%2F49%2F9e79b5794ed69ef1e557937460dd%2Fb8n2f01-182.tif 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8b6c3ab/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5400x3031+0+310/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbf%2F49%2F9e79b5794ed69ef1e557937460dd%2Fb8n2f01-182.tif 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/74c4efb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5400x3031+0+310/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbf%2F49%2F9e79b5794ed69ef1e557937460dd%2Fb8n2f01-182.tif" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="The Martin Theatre sits just past the park's main gate. Last year, Ravinia <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2025/08/09/ravinia-renovations-the-audrey-grand-reopening-2026" target="_blank" ><u>unveiled the first of its renovated venues</u></a>, the Sandra K. Crown Theater inside The Audrey, ahead of its grand reopening this past July.</p><p>Concertgoers bought tickets to see the Chicago Symphony Orchestra perform with pop artist Lizzo and classical pianist Yunchan Lim, and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/07/10/ravinia-renovation-hunter-pavilion-cso-lizzo-acoustics-architect-history-concert-tickets" target="_blank" ><u>were among the first to experience the $70 million makeover</u></a> of the park’s signature stage, the Hunter Pavilion. That update included a bigger stage, wider chairs and better acoustics — but fewer seats.</p><p>Future phases of renovations include updates to the Carousel Stage and Bennett Gordon Hall.</p>

entries.title: El 35% de hogares de Chicago, especialmente en el lado sur, tiene inseguridad alimentaria, según informe
entries.summary: <p>Se estima que el 35% de los hogares en Chicago enfrenta algún tipo de inseguridad alimentaria, según un informe publicado el lunes por el Greater Chicago Food Depository.</p><p>El depositorio, que abastece despensas de alimentos en cientos de lugares del Condado de Cook, se asoció por primera vez con NORC de la Universidad de Chicago para publicar el informe “Hunger in Chicago Report”, que detalla qué comunidades y qué tipos de hogares enfrentan algún nivel de inseguridad alimentaria, definida como patrones de alimentación interrumpidos o reducción en la cantidad de alimentos.</p><p>Los residentes de Chicago que participaron en la encuesta este verano respondieron una serie de preguntas, como si en los últimos 30 días algún miembro del hogar había omitido comidas o reducido porciones porque no había suficiente dinero.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-030000" name="module-030000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>El informe publicado el lunes indica que la inseguridad alimentaria es más generalizada de lo que señalaban informes previos. En 2024, aproximadamente el 13% de los hogares en Illinois experimentaban inseguridad alimentaria y alrededor del 24% presentaban inseguridad alimentaria marginal, según un análisis de datos del <a class="Link" href="https://ukcpr.uky.edu/resources" target="_blank" >University of Kentucky Center for Poverty Research</a>.</p><p>Kate Maehr, directora ejecutiva del Greater Chicago Food Depository, dijo que la inseguridad alimentaria que enfrenta la gente está impulsada por la inflación que eleva los precios de los comestibles y por familias que aún se están recuperando de los cambios en la economía desde la pandemia de COVID-19.</p><p>“Los datos son tan contundentes, y lo que está en juego es tan alto”, dijo Maehr. “Esto es una cuestión moral básica. Creo que la comida es un derecho humano básico, y más de un tercio de los hogares en nuestra gran ciudad tienen dificultades para acceder a algo tan básico como la alimentación”.</p><p>La mayor necesidad de alimentos se produce en medio de cambios al mayor programa de asistencia alimentaria, el Programa de Asistencia Nutricional Suplementaria (SNAP). SNAP ha navegado por requisitos laborales ampliados para los participantes y trasladará de forma dramática los costos del programa a los estados como parte del masivo plan de impuestos y gasto del presidente Donald Trump, a menudo referido como la Grande y Hermosa Ley, que se convirtió en ley el año pasado.</p><p>En Illinois, la participación en el programa federal de asistencia alimentaria ya ha caído un 16% en comparación con 2025, según el Departamento de Servicios Humanos de Illinois (IDHS). En junio, el número de personas que reciben beneficios de SNAP bajó a casi 1.6 millones —el menor número de personas recibiendo asistencia alimentaria en el estado desde 2009.</p><p>Maehr describió los cambios como “jalar la alfombra de debajo de las familias vulnerables, y le quitó este recurso crítico a tanta gente”.</p><p>La inseguridad alimentaria es particularmente pronunciada en el lado sur, donde el 51% de los residentes encuestados indicó que tenía seguridad alimentaria muy baja o baja, según el informe.</p><p>Entre los grupos raciales de la ciudad, los residentes negros reportaron el nivel más alto de inseguridad alimentaria, con un 61%, según el informe. En contraste, solo el 14% de los hogares blancos anglosajones reportaron tener acceso limitado a alimentos.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> Heights.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Dion Dawson, director ejecutivo de Dion’s Chicago Dream, ve la necesidad en toda la ciudad. La organización entrega una caja gratuita de 10 libras de verduras y frutas frescas por toda la ciudad, pero principalmente a residentes de los vecindarios de Englewood, Austin, Garfield Park y Roseland. Actualmente tienen más de 5,000 hogares en su lista de espera.</p><p>La inseguridad alimentaria está ligada a la falta de otros recursos, dijo Dawson: los residentes también enfrentan altos niveles de desempleo mientras ven una reducción en los servicios sociales y la atención médica. Por eso, para abordar la inseguridad alimentaria, las autoridades también deben mirar la creación de empleo, dijo Dawson.</p><p>“No necesariamente tenemos solo un problema de dinero; tenemos un problema de asignación cuando se trata de algunos de los recursos en la filantropía y en los servicios sociales en general”, dijo Dawson.</p><p>La encuesta también encontró que alrededor del 47% de los hogares con un niño reportaron enfrentar inseguridad alimentaria. Maehr dijo que instarán a los legisladores a hacer cambios en las políticas para abordar la inseguridad alimentaria en los niños o correr el riesgo de perder una generación.</p><p>“Los datos son tan claros sobre lo que les pasará a los niños si no tienen acceso adecuado a alimentos de calidad y nutritivos en los primeros cinco a diez años de vida”, dijo. “No es un problema de 2026 —es un problema también indicaron que quienes enfrentan inseguridad alimentaria están retrasando u omitiendo pagos de servicios públicos y atención médica. Un 29% de quienes tienen inseguridad alimentaria también está retrasando u omitiendo pagos de renta o hipoteca.</p><p>“Tienen que recurrir a este sistema, al sistema de ayuda alimentaria de emergencia, y tomar otras decisiones de prioridad, incluyendo, en algunos casos, familias que toman la decisión —padres que toman la decisión— de no alimentarse para que sus hijos puedan tener comida”, dijo Maehr. “Están tomando estas decisiones todos los días para poder salir adelante en Estados Unidos”.</p><p>Dawson, de Dion’s Chicago Dream, dijo que el informe en muchos sentidos confirma lo que él y otros que trabajan en el sistema de ayuda alimentaria de emergencia ven a diario.</p><p>“Ahora nos toca responder de una manera que pueda honrar a todos estos residentes que actualmente se ven a sí mismos con inseguridad alimentaria”, dijo Dawson.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Tommy Pham activated, Munetaka Murakami benched for all-important series finale in Cleveland
entries.summary: <p>CLEVELAND – <b>Will Venable</b> said Monday that he would “be shocked” if <b>Tommy Pham</b> returned from his calf strain to play in this week’s series in Cleveland. As recently as postgame Tuesday, the 38-year-old veteran still needed to run the bases in front of training staff in order to get medical clearance to return for this weekend’s series hosting the Detroit Tigers.</p><p>Then Pham ran into White Sox general manager <b>Chris Getz</b> in the elevator.</p><p>“I went right to the source,” Pham said. “I felt like I could help the team win today.”</p><p>Pham did indeed run the bases under the watch of training staff, but did so on Wednesday morning. A little over an hour later, he was activated off the injured list and slotted to bat cleanup against Guardians ace left-hander <b>Parker Messick</b> in an afternoon rubber match, the winner of which will end the day leading the American League Central. Terming his calf as “good enough to play,” rather than fully healed, Pham will be the designated hitter.</p><p>“You appreciate the edge and the passion that Tommy has,” said manager Will Venable. “To work himself back in here really means a lot. To have him on the field in the lineup means a lot.”</p><p>A matchup against a tough left-handed starter is essentially why Pham was signed. <b>Edgar Quero</b> was optioned once more to make room, and had only sporadically been filling the role as a bench bat against left-handed pitching in Pham’s absence. Quero said earlier this week that he intends to play winter ball in the Dominican Republic this offseason, after seeing his playing time evaporate with the White Sox this year.</p><p>In manner akin to former Sox pitcher <b>John Danks</b>, Messick possesses a great changeup that has driven better results against right-handers (.568 OPS) than left-handers (.712), but the Sox have lined up a lot of right-handed bats–Pham, <b>Randal Grichuk</b>, <b>Brenton Doyle</b>, <b>Luisangel Acuña</b>–against him.</p><p>“It's more about balancing our lineup,” Venable. “We have Messick in there for the first half of the game. We have the second half of the game to worry about too.”</p><p><b>Mune out</b></p><p>Technically, what <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/15/white-sox-with-moments-to-second-guess-after-crushing-walk-off-loss-in-cleveland-sam-antonacci-grant-taylor-brayan-rocchio-will-venable-kyle-teel-davis-martin" target="_blank" ><u>Venable contended postgame Tuesday</u></a> after Murakami went 0-for-4 with four strikeouts, is that changing his place in the batting order wouldn’t “magically fix his swing.”</p><p>So instead, Murakami–5-for-51 with 31 strikeouts in September–is just out of the lineup entirely.</p><p>“Just truthfully give him a blow,” Venable said. “As we did similarly with <b>Colson [Montgomery </b>on Tuesday] where these guys who are in spots where they’re continuing to work really hard and it’s just not coming out on the field. I know there’s a little bit of frustration there.”</p><p><b>Thorpe out too</b></p><p>Having exhausted the timeline for his rehab assignment for Tommy John surgery recovery, the White Sox optioned right-hander <b>Drew Thorpe</b> to Triple-A on Wednesday. Thorpe, who possesses a great changeup but a below-average fastball, has made six rehab starts with the Charlotte Knights (2.79 ERA in 29 innings).</p><p>With 10 games left after Wednesday and options requiring a 15-day stay in the minors, the move takes Thorpe out of consideration for a major league call-up for the rest of the season.</p><p>“So proud of him for his journey and the way that he's progressed,” said Venable of Thorpe, who has not pitched in the majors since 2024. “There's just not an opportunity here right now for him.”</p>
entries.author: James Fegan

entries.title: Bears RB D’Andre Swift named NFC Offensive Player of the Week
entries.summary: <p>Bears running back D'Andre Swift was named NFC Offensive Player of the Week on Wednesday.</p><p>In the team's 59-37 season-opening win against the Panthers in Carolina, Swift ran 18 times for 124 yards and a career-high three touchdowns. He had signed a three-year, $33.75 million contract extension two days earlier.</p><p>"He's had a good week, huh?" coach Ben Johnson said after the game.</p><p>Quarterback Caleb Williams called Swift a "golden star" on the team. </p><p>"He can do everything," Williams said. "He can catch. He can block. Obviously, he can run downhill. He can run wide zone. He can run tosses and things like that, get the edge. From there, he's not only getting first downs, he's trying to take them to the crib. He's a special player. I'm glad we have him for the next three, four years."</p><p>Swift is the first Bears running back in almost 10 years to win the award. Jordan Howard won in for Week 8 in 2016.</p><p>The Bears play the Vikings on Sunday at Soldier Field. </p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: Chicago man accused of recent sexual attacks in Avondale
entries.summary: <p>A Northwest Side man is accused of a string of sexual abuse attacks that occurred Friday in Avondale. </p><p>Zayer Picado-Sevilla, 33, was charged with felony counts of aggravated criminal sexual abuse causing bodily harm and attempted aggravated criminal sexual assault causing bodily harm in addition to driving with a never-issued license and citations for obstructing a driver's view and carrying alcohol as a driver, Chicago police said. </p><p>Those attacks occurred <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/avondale/2026/09/12/police-investigating-reported-sexual-abuse-after-women-were-attacked-in-avondale" target="_blank" >between 8 p.m. and 9 p.m. Friday</a> in the 3400 block of North Springfield Avenue, 3900 block of North Cornelia Avenue and 3300 block of North Avers Avenue, police said. Picado-Sevilla is accused of grabbing women from behind and fondling them over their clothing before fleeing.</p><p>Picado-Sevilla, of the 3500 block of North Kilbourn Avenue, is scheduled to appear at a detention hearing Wednesday at the Leighton Criminal Courthouse.</p>

entries.title: 'La Bola Negra' kicks off Reeling film festival in Chicago
entries.summary: <p>Reeling: The Chicago LGBTQ+ International Film Festival opens Thursday with the Cannes-saluted “La Bola Negra.” Oscar buzz is in the air. It’s also the first major gay film in the 44-year-old event's history, after a decades-long quest by organizers to showcase high-profile queer stories.</p><p>The nearly three-hour passionate panorama, which links three gay men in stories set before, during and after Spain’s Civil War, was written and directed by two gay men and stars three gay actors — rare for a big release. A gay-themed manuscript by Federico Garcia Lorca, a Spanish poet and playwright executed in that war, figures in the plot. He is played by a gay Madrid playwright and performance artist.</p><p>“This is unprecedented in so many ways,” Reeling founder and executive director Brenda Webb said in a Zoom interview. “An epic queer love story — those don’t come along very often.” In past years she would lobby Hollywood studios for months to screen a new gay or lesbian feature in Reeling with no luck. “Brokeback Mountain” was a nope. Webb did get “Bros,” “Bent,” “Stonewall” and “The Search for Signs of Intelligent Life in the Universe.” “When we have gotten them, they’ve not come easy to us,” she said.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-c80000" name="module-c80000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Reeling: The Chicago LGBTQ+ International Film Festival</h3><br><b>When:</b> Sept. 17-27<br><b>Where:</b> Music Box Theatre, 3733 N. Southport Ave.; Landmark Century Centre Cinema, 2828 N. Clark St.; and Chicago Filmmakers Firehouse Cinema, 1326 W. Hollywood Ave.<br><b>Tickets:</b> $15<br><b>Info:</b> <a class="Link" href="http://www.reelingfilmfest.org/" target="_blank" >reelingfilmfest.org</a></div> </div><p>Booking “La Bola Negra” culminates a “sea change” in mainstream regard of Reeling and other LGBTQ+ fests, said Webb. “Part of the difficulty is that if a distributor had a gay film, one of the reasons they didn’t want it to be an LGBTQ film festival was because they didn’t want it to be labeled ‘gay,’ even if it was gay. It’s almost like they tried to keep it a secret, right? It was a gay film, but it was kept closeted by distributors who were afraid it would limit the audience if they had called it a queer film or put it in a queer film festival.” Over time, gay and lesbian fests demonstrated there was a large audience, gay and straight. “Netflix, I think, sees the queer audience as key to the success of this film,” she noted.</p><p> Netflix picked Reeling for the local launch of “La Bola Negra.” Ticket-holders at the sold-out Music Box Theater screening on Thursday will get a first look at the likely Oscar contender. The Spanish-made subtitled film comes back to the Music Box for a 35mm theatrical run next month.</p><p>Netflix releases “La Bola Negra” in select theaters on Oct. 16 but does not start streaming the film until Dec. 2. Variety reports that “47-day exclusive window [is] the widest theatrical commitment the company has given one of its titles to date.” </p><p>“La Bola Negra” premiered in May at the Cannes Film Festival, where co-directors Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo were jointly named Best Director. The longtime collaborators co-wrote the screenplay with Spanish playwright Alberto Conejero.</p><p>“We wanted it to be a big movie to assert that LGBTQ+ stories can be big — that they don't have to appeal to just a niche audience,” Calvo told the <a class="Link" href="https://elpais.com/cultura/cine/2026-05-21/los-javis-en-cannes-federico-garcia-lorca-no-es-una-idea-sino-una-persona-a-la-que-asesinaron-por-maricon.html" target="_blank" ><u>Madrid newspaper El Pais</u></a>. “Let’s give all the straight people the war movie they want, but let’s give our community the love story that they want,” <a class="Link" href="https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-news/la-bola-negra-telluride-panel-1236692680/" target="_blank" >he told the audience at the Telluride Film Festival</a> last week, according to The Hollywood Reporter.</p><p>Touted by Chicago Filmmakers as “the second-longest-running LGBTQ+ film festival in the world,” Reeling was founded in 1981 with the goal of giving Chicago’s LGBTQ+ community the stories they wanted but were not getting from Hollywood. This year’s fest will screen 36 narrative and documentary features and 59 shorts from 22 countries at three venues from Sept. 17-27.</p><p> The nonprofit Chicago Filmmakers, now based in Edgewater, was originally located at 6 W. Hubbard St. when Webb began the festival. The 90-seat storefront theater showed 16mm shorts by experimental filmmakers such as Kenneth Anger and Barbara Hammer. “They bring in a lot of experimental work,” documentary filmmaker Gordon Quinn told the Chicago Sun-Times in 1982. “Their Lesbian and Gay Film Festival was an enormous success. It influenced film programs around the country.”</p><p>Audiences grew and offerings included more narrative and nonfiction feature-length entries by independent filmmakers. This year’s lineup includes diverse genres. Even a horror film with a Satanic ectopic pregnancy. </p><p>Here are a few to check out:</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-c60000" name="image-c60000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a48895b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4942x2774+0+261/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F4e%2F9a%2Fd755fae748efbe70cb472a5f0331%2Fkey-image-meetingmarsha-08112025-rs-9058.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/194a4e6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4942x2774+0+261/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F4e%2F9a%2Fd755fae748efbe70cb472a5f0331%2Fkey-image-meetingmarsha-08112025-rs-9058.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/eb7ceee/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4942x2774+0+261/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F4e%2F9a%2Fd755fae748efbe70cb472a5f0331%2Fkey-image-meetingmarsha-08112025-rs-9058.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Meeting Marsha behind the scenes in Sherman Oaks in Los Angeles, Ca., on Aug. 11, 2025. Clark St. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Photo by Riley N. Sims/Riley Sims Photography</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>“Meeting Marsha” </h3><p>Writer-director McKenzie Goodwin, co-host of the Two Dykes and a Mic podcast, scores a delightful L.A. comedy on queer careerism. The title’s aging TV star, the egg donor mom of a struggling playwright, shows up and upsets a lesbian wedding proposal. The screening is sponsored by Tello Films, a streamer that bills itself as “Like Netflix, but lesbian.” <i>(6:30 p.m. Sept. 23, Landmark’s Century Centre Cinema, 2828 N. Clark St. )</i></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-450000" name="image-450000"></a> entries.title: O'Hare ranks last in customer satisfaction survey
entries.summary: <p>Have O'Hare or Midway Airport seemed relatively shabby recently?</p><p>If so, you're not alone.</p><p>Both of Chicago's airports have again been ranked below average in JD Power's annual airport customer satisfaction survey.</p><p>O'Hare tied for last place with Newark Liberty Airport in New Jersey among the nation's 20 largest "mega airports."</p><p>O'Hare has ranked poorly over the last few years, but this is the first time the airport has taken last place. In 2024, O'Hare ranked 18th out of 20, then rose to 16th place last year.</p><p>JD Power surveyed 24,000 travelers from July 2025 to July 2026. The survey asked travelers to rate "ease or travel," trust in the airport, as well as staff, food and retail.</p><h3>Why did O’Hare rank so poorly?</h3><p>O'Hare ranked badly because of its ongoing concourse construction, according to Michael Taylor, J.D. Power’s managing director of travel, hospitality and retail.</p><p>O'Hare started an $8 billion terminal expansion last year. A portion of the airfield is torn up for the 19-gate satellite terminal, Concourse D, <a class="Link" href="https://cms.chicago.suntimes.com/cms/content/edit.jsp?typeId=7d984112-0772-3a35-93aa-34c50aaf2ffd&id=000001a0-ab71-d134-a5ab-bb7d707c0000" target="_blank" >expected to be completed</a> in late 2028. The city still hasn't started work on the Global Terminal expected to replace Terminal 2 by 2033.</p><p>Until the renovation is complete, O'Hare will continue to be too small for how many people it serves, Taylor said. More than <a class="Link" href="https://aci.aero/resources/busiest-airports-in-the-world/" target="_blank" >84 million passengers</a> passed through O'Hare last year.</p><p>"It's a very crowded environment," he said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b70000" entries.title: Evanston's Harley Clarke Mansion could soon become community hub
entries.summary: <p>The transformation of Evanston’s Harley Clarke Mansion — a nearly 100-year-old landmark along the lakefront — took a major step forward last week.</p><p>The Evanston Historic Preservation Commission approved Celadon Partners’ plans to turn the Harley Clarke Mansion into an event space with amenities like a coffee shop and restaurant. </p><p>“This project has been an evolution, and it's been because we've listened to the community,” Celadon Partners CEO Scott Henry said. “I think it's good, [with] time invested up front, to make sure we've got a really great project.”</p><p>About two years ago, Celadon responded to Evanston's Request for Proposals for the mansion with an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2024/09/27/developer-celadon-plan-commercial-uses-evanstons-landmark-harley-clarke-mansion" >adaptive reuse project</a> that would include a boutique hotel. </p><p>Some portions of the initial proposal, including the hotel, have been axed due to market conditions, but Henry said the team remains committed to keeping the mansion as a public asset while honoring its history. The redevelopment cost remains at $30 million, and the developer's seeking $12 million in federal and state historic tax credits.</p><p>When the event space isn't booked, it will be open for public uses such as fitness classes and co-working spaces. In addition to the restaurant and coffee shop, an ice cream parlor operated by an Evanston business will also open. And the mansion’s billiards room will become a jazz club-style speakeasy, Henry said.</p><p>Celadon will also launch Harley Clarke Beer Co. with more than a dozen beers brewed through a partner brewery in the North Side. Some of the beers, along with some cocktails, are based on recipes Celadon found in the mansion’s walls during demolition and due diligence work on the building. Henry said some of the beers will be brewed in French oak or gin barrels, giving them a taste “you just can’t get anywhere else.”</p><p>“Harley Clarke's going to be different and special, even above the amazing things we’re doing with the mansion,” Henry said. “We really want people to come back again and again because we're always going to be introducing these new, fun things that you just can't find anywhere else.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-190000" name="image-190000"></a> The mansion was built for utility magnate Harley Clarke in 1926, and the grounds, designed by renowned landscape architect Jens Jensen, were completed in 1928. Evanston landmarked the property in 1982.</p><p>Celadon is giving the nonprofit Jens Jensen Gardens in Evanston $3.5 million to restore the property’s gardens to reflect Jensen’s original vision. The nonprofit will be a lifetime partner of property to help maintain the gardens, according to Henry.</p><p>Celadon will restore the property’s coach house into a hub for the nonprofit, including offices, equipment storage and a learning center for the public. Henry said it's also mulling a program where members of the public who volunteer with the Jens Jensen Gardens, or another nonprofit, can receive food and drink discounts at the mansion.</p><p>Henry’s firm is no stranger to adaptive reuse. It’s set to begin construction on Pullman’s historic <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/02/24/gov-jb-pritzker-100-million-redevelopment-pullman-hotel-florence" >Hotel Florence</a> in March 2027, turning the site into a “mind-blowing entertainment experience.” His firm also converted the former West Pullman Elementary School into senior housing.</p><p>Henry said the Harley Clarke Mansion is in great shape compared to other historic properties his firm has worked on. </p><p>“This is a dream,” he said. “We're going to do our best to look at historic photos to try and bring back what [the mansion] was, but really … the mansion is super intact and a really nice starting point for us.”</p><p>There are “so many hidden treasures” Celadon plans to honor in the mansion’s future, Henry said. Clarke’s daughter’s bathroom is one of the most complete rooms, with original tiling depicting fairy-tales and children’s stories. The tiles are serving as the inspiration behind the ice cream parlor’s flavors, he said.</p><p>Other elements being preserved are an original copper Juliet balcony and ornate copper gutters.</p><p>Celadon still needs approvals from the Evanston Land Use Commission and the City Council. </p><p>The firm hopes to start work in March 2027 and kick off operations in the first quarter of 2028.</p><p>In the meantime, Celadon has hosted pop-ups ranging from a weekend coffee stand to ice cream and beer garden events on the mansion’s east lawn. Watch parties for Northwestern University and the Bears games are also taking place in the beer garden.</p><p>The attendance at its events has affirmed to Celadon how much the community values the mansion, Nick Jefferson, director of community development and engagement at Celadon, said.</p><p>“There's so many different people that are just using the space like a public park,” Jefferson said. “When you turn around in the back and see the beer garden, it literally feels like a hidden treasure. Folks are super excited about what's to come.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2024/09/27/developer-celadon-plan-commercial-uses-evanstons-landmark-harley-clarke-mansion" >Developer’s plan would usher commercial uses into Evanston’s landmark Harley Clarke Mansion</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
entries.author: Abby Miller

entries.title: Federal Reserve hikes key interest rate for first time in 3 years, defying Trump demands for a cut
entries.summary: <p>The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate Wednesday for the first time since 2023 in an effort to quell stubbornly high inflation, a move that could spur a sharp response from the White House.</p><p>The quarter-point increase lifts the Fed’s key rate to about 3.9% and, over time, could result in higher borrowing costs for mortgages, auto loans and credit cards. In a set of quarterly projections, the Fed also signaled that its rate-setting committee expects to hike rates a second time later this year to 4.1%.</p><p>“Today’s policy action will support a timelier return” to the central bank’s 2% inflation goal, the Fed said in a statement.</p><p>The move comes as Americans are already struggling with high costs for groceries, gas and housing. Affordability has taken on a leading role in the upcoming midterm elections, just seven weeks away.</p><p>In a press conference following the Fed's announcement, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said that while the job market remains resilient, inflation has stubbornly remained above the Fed's 2% target for years. </p><p>"The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Warsh said.</p><p>Since taking the lead at the Fed in May, Warsh has said the Fed is firmly committed to taming inflation, and policymakers would take their cues from the data to determine if inflation was going in the right direction. </p><p>“We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective clearly and at sufficient speed. Today the FOMC decided that this standard has not been satisfied,” Warsh said, referring to the policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee.</p><p>The rate hike marks a turnaround for Warsh, who often suggested last year that the Fed could reduce its key rate, echoing President Donald Trump's call for lower borrowing costs.</p><p>Yet the ongoing disruptions from the Iran war, which have pushed up average gas prices more than 7% from just a month ago, threaten to spread through the economy and keep broader inflation stubbornly high. An inflation report last week showed core prices, which exclude food and energy, accelerated a bit in August.</p><p>According to the Fed’s preferred measure, inflation was 3.7% in July compared with a year ago, up from 2.3% in April 2025, just before Trump unveiled sweeping tariffs. Core inflation, which excludes the volatile food and energy categories, was 3.3% in July, the latest data available, up from 3% just before the Iran war and far above the Fed’s target.</p><p>Earlier Wednesday, the government said retail sales jumped 1.2% in August from the previous month, a sign that consumers are still spending at healthy levels despite sentiment surveys indicating Americans remain gloomy about the economy. Strong spending is a sign that interest rates at current levels aren’t necessarily restricting the economy and cooling inflation.</p><p>“While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient,” the Fed said, a likely reference to ongoing consumer spending and strong investment in AI data centers by large technology companies.</p><p>Higher inflation isn’t all about gas prices. Ongoing investment in AI has driven up prices for computer chips and other electronic gear, adding to overall inflation. Tariffs may still be elevating some costs, such as appliances, which jumped in price last month.</p><p>Trump harshly criticized Warsh’s predecessor, Jerome Powell, for not cutting rates quickly enough. The Justice Department even launched a criminal investigation into Powell over brief testimony he delivered to Congress last year, though that probe was eventually dropped.</p><p>When asked Wednesday how Trump might react to the rate increase, Warsh said, “I’ve got nothing for you on a discussion with the president.”</p><p>Kevin Hassett, Trump’s top economic adviser, was asked in an interview with Fox News on Sunday how Trump might react to a rate hike.</p><p>“I’m sure he’s not going to be super happy about it, but he will defend the independence of Kevin Warsh above all,” Hassett said.</p><p>Warsh might also have a measure of protection because his father-in-law is Ronald Lauder, a friend of Trump's and a billionaire donor to his campaigns.</p><p>In the Fed's economic projections issued along with the rate decision, officials indicated they are likely to raise the key rate once more this year. Analysts doubt that will be at the next meeting in October.</p><p>“Most FOMC members see a total of two hikes this year per the [projections], and it will likely skip October’s meeting given its proximity to the midterm elections,” Kay Haigh, of Goldman Sachs, said.</p><p>For their part, Wall Street investors have forecast three hikes for the Fed, with additional increases in December and March.</p>

entries.title: Mayor Johnson wins Round One in fight over protections for tenants
entries.summary: <p>A key concession helped Mayor Brandon Johnson win an early skirmish Wednesday in the battle for the hearts, minds and votes of Chicago’s 600,000 renters, but the political victory may not last.</p><p>The City Council’s Housing Committee chaired by one of the mayor’s closest City Council allies narrowly approved by a vote of 12 to 9 Johnson’s newly revised “Protecting Renters Ordinance” after the mayor dropped the "just cause" provision that would have required landlords to make relocation payments to tenants evicted through no fault of their own.</p><p>Elimination of that provision was only the latest change made by Johnson. He had previously exempted from the proposed ordinance owner-occupied buildings of six-flats or less. </p><p>An early draft of the mayor’s ordinance also would have required $10,000 in compensation to tenants forced to move out to avoid “unconscionable rent increases.” That provision was removed amid complaints that it could be a dangerous first step toward rent control, which would require a change in state law. </p><p>None of those changes were enough to satisfy the opposition faction led by Zoning Committee Chair Gilbert Villegas (36th), which has proposed an alternative set of renter protections favored by some of the same real estate interests that spent millions to defeat Johnson’s “Bring Chicago Home” referendum.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/07/27/renters-protection-ordinances-mayor-brandon-johnson-aldermanic-opponents-dueling-versions-chicago-city-council" >Chicago renters’ rights are at stake in dueling City Hall proposals</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>“This is going to raise rents. That’s something that our colleagues cannot support at a time when affordability is an issue,” Villegas told the Sun-Times. “We see this as no different than Trump’s tariffs. We see this as a rent tariff, which will be passed on to the renters.”</p><p>On Thursday, Villegas plans to push his alternative ordinance through the Zoning Committee he chairs. That will set the stage for the full City Council to either choose between the dueling ordinances or defer action on both and keep talking in hopes of finding common ground.</p><p>“The mayor is using this as an opportunity to try to sway people. Half the city are renters. He wants to get them activated for the election. We’re looking at it from a more pragmatic approach, whereas the mayor is looking at it from a political approach," Villegas said.</p><p>Ald. Byron Sigcho-Lopez (25th) replied that if anyone is “playing politics and showing it,” it’s Villegas, by “introducing a housing ordinance in a committee that has little jurisdiction over tenant rights” in an attempt to “create confusion and chaos.”</p><p>“I’m not sure what Ald. Villegas is doing in Zoning, but it clearly is overstepping and I’m suspecting it’s because of the money that he’s getting from the real estate industry,” Sigcho-Lopez said. </p><p>Johnson has heralded the ordinance as the first rewrite in 40 years of the Landlord Tenants Ordinance championed by former Mayor Harold Washington.</p><p>His measure would establish a rental registry to log who owns the city’s more than 500,000 rental units, and whether those landlords are complying with the law. That measure was included in Johnson’s proposal in reaction to a<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/09/05/chicago-landlords-renters-property-management-llc" > WBEZ/Chicago Sun-Times story</a> about how landlords often set up limited liability companies to mask who they are — creating an anonymity that makes it hard to hold problem landlords accountable.</p><p>The mayor’s ordinance would also create a new Bureau of Rental Housing Services to establish and enforce new standards that landlords need to follow to guarantee safe and sanitary living conditions. A so-called “Renters Bill of Rights” would require landlords to clearly explain all fees, ban move-in fees and require landlords to choose between monthly and annual pet fees.</p><p></p><p>To bankroll the new level of bureaucracy, the ordinance includes an annual registration fee of $20 per unit that’s expected to raise the $22 million in annual revenue needed to cover inspections, attorneys and other enforcement costs.</p><p>The mayor’s office maintains that the Department of Buildings “doesn’t have the manpower to enforce rental violations on top of all of the other things they’re doing.” Villegas strongly disagreed.</p><p>“At a time when we’re seeing an $882 million deficit for 2027, now’s the time to create a whole new bureau of more employees, more pension liability and add more red tape where you have duplicative services by this whole new department?” Villegas said.</p><p>Villegas' ordinance has some similarities, but also many differences. There is no registration fee, no rental housing bureau, no Tenant Bill of Rights and no new hirings, among other things. Nor would "junk" fees be banned.</p><p></p><p> At the committee meeting, building owners condemned the mayor’s revised plan as a “rent increase ordinance.”</p><p></p><p>“By adding 100 or so rules and regulations, it’s gonna be too much for many of our owners and the temptation is going to be to sell” to buyers who are “not local,” including hedge funds, said Michael Glasser, president of the Neighborhood Building Owners Alliance. </p><p></p><p></p><p>Julie Dworkin, co-executive director of the Institute for the Public Good, countered that Chicago rents have increased by 9.5% since 2023, which she called the “highest increase in the country.”</p><p></p>

entries.title: Bears report: Tackle Darnell Wright sits out with knee injury
entries.summary: <p>What happened Wednesday at Halas Hall:</p><h3>Wright sits</h3><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" >Bears</a> right tackle Darnell Wright did not practice while he deals with a knee injury.</p><p>Wright played every snap Sunday but has dealt with a right elbow injury dating to last season, when he put on a brace rather than opting for surgery. He tweaked the elbow in practice last month but didn’t miss any significant practice time.</p><p>Neville Gallimore sat out with an illness and fellow defensive tackle Grady Jarrett got a veteran rest day. Six players were limited: running backs Kyle Monangai (hamstring) and D'Andre Swift (ankle/knee), defensive lineman Dayo Odeyingbo (shoulder), cornerback Malik Muhammad (ankle), tackle Ozzy Trapilo (knee) and safety Xavier Woods (groin).</p><h3>Meanwhile, in Minneapolis </h3><p>Vikings quarteback Kyler Murray, who was concussed Sunday, was limited in practice. The team has not yet ruled him out for Sunday's game. Running back Jordan Mason, who led the team in carries and rushing yards in Week 1, will be put on injured reserve with a broken thumb. </p><h3>Swift honored</h3><p>Swift was named NFC Offensive Player of the Week on Wednesday, three days after running 18 times for 124 yards and a career-high three touchdowns. He had signed a three-year, $33.75 million contract extension two days earlier.</p><p>Swift became the first Bears running back to win the award since Jordan Howard in 2006.<br></p>

entries.title: Joven embarazada pierde al bebé y podría no volver a caminar tras ser baleada por compañero de clase en La Villita
entries.summary: <p>Una joven embarazada de 16 años de edad perdió a su bebé y podría no volver a caminar después de que un compañero de clase supuestamente le disparara en la espalda tras haberla acosado a principios de este mes en La Villita, dijeron los fiscales del Condado de Cook.</p><p>Angel David Funez Reyes, de 17 años, fue acusado de agresión agravada (delito grave) y de uso ilícito de un arma (delito menor), según dijo la Policía de Chicago en un comunicado y un portavoz de la oficina de la Fiscal del Condado de Cook. La policía había indicado anteriormente que fue procesado como menor.</p><p>Un juez ordenó que Funez Reyes permanezca detenido mientras espera juicio en el edificio de la Corte Penal Leighton durante una audiencia de detención el martes.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-230000" name="module-230000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Los fiscales dicen que Funez Reyes había estado acosando a la joven durante semanas en una clase que compartían en la escuela, preguntándole sobre su afiliación a pandillas.</p><p>También se le imputa que le mostró un arma a la joven y a su novio seis horas antes del tiroteo, según los fiscales.</p><p>Cuando ella y otra joven vieron más tarde a Funez Reyes alrededor de las 7:11 p.m. del 7 de septiembre en la cuadra 2200 al sur de Sawyer Avenue, hubo una discusión. Fue entonces cuando ella empezó a preguntar por un arma que él llevaba oculta en una sudadera con capucha.</p><p>Cuando la víctima se dio la vuelta para alejarse, Funez Reyes presuntamente le disparó una vez en la espalda antes de huir en un vehículo negro que estaba estacionado cerca, dijeron los fiscales. La joven fue llevada en estado grave al Hospital Mount Sinai para recibir tratamiento.</p><p>Los fiscales dijeron que probablemente la joven no volverá a caminar y que perdió el embarazo como resultado de sus heridas.</p><p>Funez Reyes también enfrenta cargos por robo de vehículo. Los fiscales indicaron que fue retirado de la vigilancia electrónica el 18 de agosto y que se le impuso un toque de queda de 9 p.m.</p><p>Funez Reyes había sido arrestado dos días antes del tiroteo por agresión agravada, uso ilícito de un arma, posesión de munición y obstrucción de identificación, después de que presuntamente amenazara a personas con una navaja multiusos mientras gritaba insultos relacionados con pandillas, según los fiscales.</p><p>Los fiscales afirmaron que le mintió a la policía sobre su identidad durante ese arresto, cuando se le encontraron dos cartuchos de munición y la navaja. Funez Reyes comparecerá en la corte por esos cargos el 25 de septiembre.</p><p>Funez Reyes debe volver a comparecer en la corte el 7 de octubre por el tiroteo contra la joven, dijeron las autoridades.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: The Ben Johnson-Brian Flores chess match is the best in the NFL
entries.summary: <p>The premier play-calling matchup in the NFL — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/15/chicago-bears-caleb-williams-ben-johnson-minnesota-vikings-kyler-murray-carson-wentz-nfl-week-2" target="_blank" >Ben Johnson</a> vs. Brian Flores — is entering its fourth season.</p><p>There are enough data points, then, for Johnson to think about — and overthink — all this week. The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> coach wonders what Flores thinks Johnson thinks Flores is thinking about.</p><p>“I’m on that path right now,” Johnson said with a smirk Wednesday.</p><p>Three days after scoring a whopping 59 points against the Panthers, Johnson has moved his focus onto the NFL’s most dangerous defensive coordinator. What happened in Week 1, he said, doesn’t matter when the Bears take the field for their home opener Sunday against the Vikings.</p><p>“We haven't put up any points this week,” he said.</p><p>Johnson has won his chess matches against the Vikings’ blitz-crazy defensive coordinator, both in his days as the Lions’ offensive coordinator and last season as the Bears head coach. Johnson is 5-1 lifetime against the Vikings as the play-caller, averaging a whopping 27½ points. To get there, Johnson spent countless days — and nights — trying to predict what Flores will throw at him on Sundays.</p><p>In Sunday’s dizzying comeback win against the Packers, Flores blitzed a whopping 72% of the time. Last season, the Vikings led the NFL by blitzing on 44% of their downs. It’s a safe bet that Flores will blitz the Bears like mad, too — except for that one time he didn’t. In Week 1 last year, he was content to sit back and make Caleb Williams try to pick the Vikings apart, blitzing just 32% of the snaps. In their second matchup last year, the Vikings blitzed two-thirds of the time.</p><p>The Bears lost the Week 1 matchup and won in Week 11.</p><p>“You'd like to think he's put everything he could possibly do on tape until you play him next, and you realize he hasn't yet,” Johnson said. “So it'll be something new. There always is with him, and that's what makes him such a good coordinator. It's a great challenge. It really is. You have a lot of fun on game day. Now the week of preparation is not so much fun, but you know, there's a lot of back and forth that goes into it."</p><p>Flores blitzes from so many places — from over the center to the cornerback and everywhere in between — that Johnson will spend his week trying to give quarterback Caleb Williams all the answers to Sunday’s test.</p><p>“When you go against a guy like this, you've got everything,” Johnson said. “So, that's where it's a lot. For our players, they have to really dedicate themselves over the course of the week to have success.”</p><p>Johnson needs to make sure he’s ready to pivot, too. In previous games against Flores, he said, he’s had to keep his head in the NFL-issued iPad on the sideline more than he would have liked.</p><p>“If he gets us on something, that's fine,” he said. “Then we, we got to, you know, come together and make sure we get it corrected and we'll move on from there.”</p><p>Flores is doing the exact same thing, but in reverse, this week. Tuesday, he detailed how Johnson’s offense can resemble any number of schemes, depending on his mood — from ground-and-pound to run-and-shoot, four receiver sets to run-pass options. He has no more an idea of what to expect from Johnson than the Bears coach does from him.</p><p>“So what are we getting week to week? It’s hard to know,” said Flores, who interviewed for the Bears head coaching job that went to Johnson. “And so a lot of the game is adjustments …We’re going to have our own game plan to start things off. It’s the same thing on his end — What are they doing? And how are we going to counteract what they’re doing?</p><p>“It’s certainly a chess match.”</p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: Cubs adjust Dansby Swanson's rehab plan, keep him on track to return Friday
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs </a>shortstop Dansby Swanson racked up the air miles for a rehab assignment that never happened.</p><p>For the last step in his recovery from a strained left oblique, Swanson flew to Omaha on Monday to play in Triple-A Iowa’s game Tuesday. It got rained out, and the game Wednesday appeared to be in jeopardy.</p><p>Swanson returned to Chicago on Tuesday night, and the Cubs organized a simulated game for him Wednesday at Wrigley Field. He totaled six at-bats against two prospects, right-hander Gavin Hollowell and lefty Riley Martin, who were flown in because their rehab outings also were washed out in Omaha. Swanson also played in the field.</p><p>He came out of it all just fine. Swanson will have one more workout Thursday at Wrigley before the Cubs leave for Cincinnati. They expect to activate him from the injured list Friday for the opener of the three-game series.</p><p>“I don’t think anyone could’ve predicted everything that happened,” Swanson said. “It’s one of those scenarios where we have to make the next-best decision we can. They were really thoughtful about the ways they wanted to go about it to get me as prepared as possible to be able to play.</p><p>“I feel good. I was able to do everything today with no issues.”</p><p>Swanson suffered the injury Aug. 16 on a swing. He had never strained an oblique before.</p><p>“With any oblique thing, it’s always around your ribs,” he said. “It was pretty painful in the beginning. Over the course of time, it gets healed up; then you start to feel better. You just stick to the progressions. Whatever they put in front of me I went at as best and as hard as I could.”</p><p>Swanson said he got stir-crazy during his recovery, adding that he understood why manager Craig Counsell is always moving in the dugout during games.</p><p>“I don’t really like to sit down. I’m always on the move,” he said. “Watching is a lot harder than playing.</p><p>“Honestly, I missed competing. Competing and being a part of something is so much fun. I feel like that’s why I always go into coach mode, still really be invested in the guys and helping anyone as best as I can.”</p><p>Swanson’s return will put back together the Cubs’ best infield alignment, with Nico Hoerner returning to second base. It also likely puts impressive rookie Pedro Ramirez on the bench.</p>

entries.title: Tres millennials están creando un espacio artístico cerca del arco de La Villita
entries.summary: <p>Para la ocupada temporada del arte en otoño, Daniel Silva quería que su nuevo espacio de exhibición y centro cultural <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/tequ_co/" target="_blank" >Te-Qu</a> estuviera abierto y listo para funcionar en La Villita.</p><p>Su equipo, que incluye al muralista local <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/mr.pintamuro/?hl=en" target="_blank" >Mr. Pintamuro</a> y a Julio Anaya, de <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/littlevillagelocal/?hl=en" target="_blank" >Little Village Local</a>, planeó una gran inauguración para el 30 de julio. La celebración iba a incluir dignatarios locales, un DJ, servicio de catering y más, todo como parte de una gran reunión comunitaria.</p><p>Pero un día antes del evento, el Departamento de Asuntos Comerciales y Protección al Consumidor informó a los líderes de Te-Qu que no podía emitir una licencia comercial porque la propiedad, por alguna razón, está ubicada en una zona residencial.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-af0000" name="module-af0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Ahora, el espacio llega a la temporada del arte en otoño con una variedad de pop-ups planeados y colaboraciones con negocios vecinos y vendedores ambulantes a lo largo de la calle 26. Como la mayoría de sus grandes eventos comunitarios se realizan los fines de semana, han puesto en marcha una serie de murales rotativos y planean organizar exposiciones con artistas locales en un entries.title: Chicago police supervisor who led botched Anjanette Young raid should be fired, appeals court rules
entries.summary: <p>An appeals court panel has upheld a decision to fire the Chicago police supervisor in charge of the botched raid in 2019 that led to social worker Anjanette Young being handcuffed naked in her home.</p><p>The decision came down last week, with the appeals court affirming the Chicago Police Board’s finding that Sgt. Alex Wolinski’s inability to lead or intervene “allowed the horrible treatment of Ms. Young to occur and continue.”</p><p>The board voted in June 2023 to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2023/6/15/23763033/anjanette-young-chicago-police-board-alex-wolinski-botched-raid" target="_blank" >discharge Wolinski</a> from the police department, finding his actions led to “public distrust and a lack of confidence in the integrity of the Chicago Police Department.” In a 31-page ruling, the board specifically cited Wolinski’s “failure of leadership.”</p><p>Wolinski fought the decision by filing a complaint with the city. Then, when a Cook County judge sided with the board in October 2024, Wolinski appealed. Wolinski said he made “a reasoned, although inappropriate, judgment when faced with a chaotic and emotionally charged situation,” according to the appellate ruling.</p><p>But the appeals court found Wolinski’s firing wasn’t “arbitrary and unreasonable," as he had claimed.</p><p>The city’s Law Department said the court “appropriately upheld the Police Board’s findings that Wolinski exhibited extremely serious and substantial shortcomings in connection with executing the warrant, and that his conduct warranted discharge.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-credit"><p>CBS 2 Chicago</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Young was undressed and getting ready for bed when police burst into her home in February 2019 looking for a man with a gun.</p><p>Wolinski, who had been with the department since 2002, allowed Young to remain in handcuffs and naked for 40 minutes in a room full of male police officers. She remained in that position even after officers determined they were at the wrong home.</p><p>In 2021, a day after the Civilian Office of Police Accountability released its findings on the raid, then-police Supt. David Brown <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2021/11/10/22774338/anjanette-young-botched-chicago-police-raid-sgt-alex-wolinski-copa-civilian-office-accountability" target="_blank" >moved to fire Wolinski</a>.</p><p>That same year, Young sued the city and 12 officers involved. She received a $2.9 million settlement and has since become <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/city-hall/2025/02/21/anjanette-young-victim-of-an-infamous-2019-wrongful-chicago-police-raid-marks-another-year-without-reform" target="_blank" >an outspoken advocate for police reform.</a></p><p>In April, she was selected to serve on the Community Commission for Public Safety and Accountability, the oversight body now charged with finding a new police superintendent.</p><p>Wolinski’s lawyer didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Wolinski now works for the Niles Police Department, state records show.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2023/6/15/23763033/anjanette-young-chicago-police-board-alex-wolinski-botched-raid" target="_blank" >In botched Anjanette Young raid, Chicago Police Board votes to fire sergeant in charge</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2021/11/10/22774338/anjanette-young-botched-chicago-police-raid-sgt-alex-wolinski-copa-civilian-office-accountability" target="_blank" >CPD sergeant should be fired over botched Anjanette Young raid, top cop says; other officers also face discipline</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2020/12/16/22178628/chicago-police-raid-video-social-worker-anjanette-young-black-caucus-calls-investigation" target="_blank" >‘I want accountability,’ says woman seen in video of botched CPD raid</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Cubs are inconsistent, but ‘still feel like we can absolutely be the last team standing’
entries.summary: <p>Welcome to crunch time for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>.</p><p>With only a handful of games remaining on the regular-season schedule and a tight NL wild-card race keeping their playoff fate a mystery, where does this team stand in terms of being able to achieve its long-held, championship-level goals?</p><p>It depends on who you ask.</p><p>The folks in the Wrigley Field bleachers have different thoughts than the ones in the third-base dugout.</p><p>Inconsistency has struck at, seemingly, the worst time for these Cubs, who still have baseball’s highest-scoring offense and far and away its best defense but haven’t been able to display regular dominance down the stretch.</p><p>The Brewers ran away with the NL Central, again, and series wins have been few since the middle of August.</p><p>And then <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/15/cubs-bullpen-braves-loss-jacob-webb-edward-cabrera-craig-counsell-playoffs" >there’s that bullpen</a>.</p><p>At this exact moment, it might be hard to convince fans that this team is bound for October glory.</p><p>These Cubs, though, with their focus squarely on a deep playoff run <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/25/cubs-playoffs-brewers-pirates-nl-central-matthew-boyd-starting-rotation" >since last year’s postseason exit</a>, don’t need to be sold.</p><p>“I don’t think we’ve ever lost sight of what our potential is. We still feel like we can absolutely be the last team standing,” designated hitter Michael Conforto said Wednesday. “Regardless of what the standings say or what’s going on in the division, it doesn’t change the fact that we feel like we can win the rest of the series through the end of October.</p><p>“We have the experience and the mindset that that’s what it takes to be the last team standing: focus on winning the series the rest of the way. And then you get a ring at the end. I don’t think that confidence has ever been lost.”</p><p>Conforto, though he had a disappointing campaign at the plate and didn’t play in the postseason, was part of the last group to get rings at season’s end, last year’s Dodgers, who won their second straight World Series title.</p><p>He’s seen up close what it takes to win it all, and he’s said throughout the summer that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/25/cubs-michael-conforto-pinch-hitter-stats-dodgers-world-series-craig-counsell-ian-happ" >he sees that special something in the Cubs</a>.</p><p>But assembling the ingredients and baking the cake are two very different tasks.</p><p>Winning every series from here till the end of October seems a tall task for a team that came into Wednesday’s rubber game with the Braves having won only three of its previous nine series.</p><p>It takes quality in all areas to be what Conforto said, the last team standing.</p><p>Can the Cubs, tops in offense and defense but struggling on the pitching front, deliver?</p><p>“We know exactly what we have here, we just have to play the game well,” Conforto said. “There’s been games that we haven’t. We continue to learn from that.</p><p>“At the end of the day, if you want to win the World Series, you have to play really well down the stretch and through the playoffs. That’s what we’re focused on: just trying to show up every day and play the game well.”</p><p>Though the Cubs have been inconsistent on the field of late, they’ve been consistent behind the scenes all season. The most frequent compliment handed out is their focus on each new day, their ability to not get dragged down by the emotion of a loss or overly heightened by the emotion of a win.</p><p>Good thing, too, because these Cubs have had a wild roller-coaster ride of a campaign, including this latest dip.</p><p>“There’s obviously been some really high highs,” Conforto said, “and there’s been some pretty low lows, as well.”</p><p>Will the remainder of September bring highs or lows?</p><p>Time to find out.</p><p>“When the emotion gets heightened and there’s more energy surrounding every game … that energy comes when you’re in it and you have a chance to do something special,” Conforto said. “Fans get frustrated when they know how good the team is [and the team doesn’t perform like it].</p><p>“All the energy means good things. We understand that. We see it, we feel it, but we do have the ability to go out and focus on the job. That’s just kind of a unique thing for this group.”</p>

entries.title: Sky's Courtney Vandersloot wasn’t the closer she hoped to be, but shouldn’t have to fill that role next year
entries.summary: <p>With four games left in the regular season, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky’s</a> focus will be on developing young players and building for the future rather than a postseason run.</p><p>It’s not where this team wanted to be.</p><p>Everyone expected this roster, built around legendary point guard Courtney Vandersloot, to make the playoffs.</p><p>Say what you want about the decision to build a team around a 37-year-old — and the critiques will continue until the Sky are winning again — but Vandersloot does not shy away from acknowledging her shortcomings.</p><p>She’s owned up to the Sky's struggles in close games <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/07/04/sky-rally-late-then-let-another-one-slip-away-in-overtime-loss-to-aces" >all season long</a>, including in an interview with the Sun-Times on Tuesday.</p><p>“I think I had opportunities where the ball was in my hands to make plays for us down the stretch in a couple games, and I don’t think I had the right decision-making ability at the time,” she said. “Or my comfortability in those moments was not what it was used to being.”</p><p>“I think part of it was just not playing, not having a lot of ‘big moment’ reps. I feel like I never really got to be myself.”</p><p>Vandersloot returned to Chicago to help lift the Sky back to the playoff standard that existed when she departed in 2022, but an ACL tear early in the 2025 season interrupted that. When she returned this season, she lacked the end-of-game heroics she was known for back in 2022.</p><p>Overall, she doesn’t feel like she “impacted winning” as much as she wanted to.</p><p>Some aspects of her game certainly declined; her finishing at the rim is 10 percentage points lower than it was in her prime, and quicker guards keep targeting her defensively.</p><p>But you don’t lose 15 clutch games because of one person. Nearly every starter had a fatal blunder at some point, and the blame for this season should spread from the top all the way down.</p><p>Now the focus turns to next season. The roster is likely to look similar, with 9 of 13 players effectively under contract. Vandersloot still has faith in the potential of this group, and she believes that using the offseason to rehab can take her own performance to another level.</p><p>“My knee is in a good spot, but I came back with the idea that this was part of my ‘return to play,’ and now I want it to be like a ‘return to perform,’” she said. “I’m out there performing and excelling … at the level that I think I can play that.”</p><p>“For me, it’s just being able to put myself in a better place to help this team win.”</p><p>Many aspects of Vandersloot’s recovery were encouraging. Her return in late June gave the offense an instant boost, with the team scoring a franchise-record 124 points. Her individual production since returning is in line with where she left off in 2025 — 9 points on 43.3% shooting to go along with 5.2 assists.</p><p>Getting more comfortable in end-of-game scenarios will help. But rather than trying to get back to her old self, success for Vandersloot next season may also include adjusting to a more complementary role.</p><p>Star forward Rickea Jackson will be returning from an ACL injury and is just the kind of shot-creator you want to give the ball to at the end of games. Sydney Taylor has also revealed her clutch gene, becoming the first player to hit multiple buzzer-beating threes in a season since Vandersloot in 2022.</p><p>Developing those two youngsters as closers should be the priority next season.</p><p>If she’s willing, Vandersloot can take a little bit of pressure off herself and settle into being more of a shepherd rather than a savior.</p><p>Of course for an all-time great competitor, that’s easier said than done.</p>
