entries.title: Jury weighs case of customs officer accused of sexual assaults — after prosecutor slams his 'rape joke'
entries.summary: <p>Minutes into his final argument to jurors Wednesday, a defense attorney for U.S. Customs and Border Protection Officer<b> </b>Luis Uribe<b> </b>brought up “the statement …<b> </b>that I know you all heard, and I know you all thought about.”</p><p>He meant Uribe’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/15/cbp-officer-tells-jury-he-met-sex-workers-but-never-raped-anyone-then-brags-he-got-a-good-workout-in" target="_blank" >quip on the witness stand</a> a day earlier, as Uribe defended himself at trial against claims of sexual assault. When a prosecutor asked Uribe about one alleged assault, Uribe remarked that he “got a good workout in” and insisted the encounter was consensual.</p><p>It took defense attorney Michael Clancy<b> </b>less than 10 minutes to assure jurors<b> </b>during closing arguments Wednesday<b> </b>his client had given a “horrible answer”<b> </b>— born out of frustration.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/15/cbp-officer-tells-jury-he-met-sex-workers-but-never-raped-anyone-then-brags-he-got-a-good-workout-in" >Customs officer tells jury he met sex workers but ‘never raped anyone,’ then cracks crude joke</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>But prosecutors seized on it.</p><p>“He made jokes,” Assistant U.S. Attorney Jonathan<b> </b>Shih<b> </b>told the jury. “Actually, he made a rape joke. Actually, he compared the rape … to a workout.</p><p>“I think that’s all you need to know about the defendant.”</p><p>Now federal jurors are considering Uribe’s fate, after hearing days of evidence that he <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/12/09/ohare-based-border-patrol-officer-sexually-abused-robbed-women-in-2022-indictment-claims" target="_blank" >robbed and sexually assaulted</a> four women<b> </b>in Chicago’s suburbs between February and October 2022, when he was based at O’Hare Airport. The women were Chinese immigrants who spoke little English and had apparent ties to the sex work industry.</p><p>“Despite their trauma, despite their fears, four women — four victims — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/10/customs-border-protection-luis-uribe-rape-schaumburg" target="_blank" >bravely came forward</a> to tell the truth about what he did,” Shih told the jury. “And what he did was unleash long-lasting devastation upon these women.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/10/customs-border-protection-luis-uribe-rape-schaumburg" >In CBP officer’s rape trial, woman describes alleged attack at Schaumburg hotel: ‘He showed a badge’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The jury retired to consider the case a little after 1 p.m. Wednesday, and they left for the day around 4:30 p.m. Deliberations are expected to continue Thursday.</p><p>Uribe is charged with 10 counts of deprivation of civil rights under color of law and one count of brandishing a firearm during a crime of violence. He’s been in federal custody since his arrest last December, and the charges threaten to put him away<b> </b>for the rest of his life.</p><p>So with his freedom on the line, Uribe took the stand Tuesday. He admitted visiting prostitutes. But he denied raping anyone and said he had consensual sex with the women. He said a fifth woman, who also testified, had threatened to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/09/luis-uribe-cbp-border-protection-sexual-assault" target="_blank" >set him up</a><b> </b>if he didn’t help with her immigration issues.</p><p>Then, during cross-examination, Shih asked Uribe about using “physical fitness time”<b> </b>to leave work early for one of the encounters in question.</p><p>“You didn’t go to the gym,” Shih remarked.</p><p>“I still got a good workout in,” Uribe told him.</p><p>“You’re describing the rape … as a good workout?” the prosecutor shot back.</p><p>“It wasn’t a rape,” Uribe retorted. “It was consensual sex.”</p><p>Clancy on Wednesday asked jurors to “remember what [Uribe] had gone through”<b> </b>before making that comment. He said Uribe sat through more than a week of trial and had “had enough.”</p><p>“He was frustrated by all the lies,” Clancy said. “He was frustrated by all the accusations.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/09/luis-uribe-cbp-border-protection-sexual-assault" >Border Protection officer accused of sex assaults became ‘perfect mark’ for prostitution ring, lawyer says</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>And, Clancy told jurors, they “can’t consider that he said something so crass.”</p><p>“He may not be someone you like,” Clancy said. “He may not be someone that you are real happy was a law enforcement officer. … [But] they have not proved beyond a reasonable doubt that he robbed or raped anyone.”</p><p>Prosecutors argued otherwise, largely based on the testimony of Uribe’s four accusers. Shih and Assistant U.S. Attorney Richard<b> </b>Rothblatt<b> </b>pointed to evidence they said corroborated the women’s testimony, even though it was sometimes contradictory or unclear.</p><p>Rothblatt argued the discrepancies show “these victims are doing their best to recall what happened to them under traumatic circumstances.”</p><p>And, he compared their demeanor on the witness stand<b> </b>to Uribe’s.</p><p>One accuser, Rothblatt said, “was breathlessly crying … such that her vision was clouded. We had to clear the courtroom.”</p><p>But to Uribe, Rothblatt said, “that was just a good workout.”</p>

entries.title: Five storylines for Blackhawks training camp: Connor Bedard, Ethan Del Mastro and more
entries.summary: <p>For the past couple weeks, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> coach Jeff Blashill and his staff have only been able to watch their players skate and scrimmage from afar.</p><p>On Thursday morning, they'll finally get hands-on for the first on-ice day of the NHL's shortened training camps, following an off-ice day Wednesday.</p><p>The Hawks will race through their systems prep, new emphases and four-game preseason slate to prepare for their Sept. 29 season opener in Las Vegas, which is less than two weeks away.</p><p>Here are five storylines to follow:</p><h3><b>Bedard’s rehab</b></h3><p>The Hawks got their Connor Bedard <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/09/15/connor-bedard-blackhawks-captain-best-player-face-of-franchise-leadership" target="_blank" >captain announcement</a> out of the way before camp, so the focus on Bedard will shift entirely to his rehab from <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/07/08/blackhawks-connor-bedard-shoulder-surgery-injury-timeline" target="_blank" >left shoulder surgery</a>.</p><p>On July 8, he was given a four-month recovery estimate, which equated to early November. He said Tuesday he's unsure what his timeline looks like now. He confirmed he won't be ready for the start of the season, but he hopes to "get back as soon as possible."</p><p>He has been skating individually and lightly shooting. When will he begin skating with the team? When will he begin shooting with them? And when will he be cleared for contact? Those answers will be illuminating.</p><h3><b>Roster math</b></h3><p>One consequence of the shortened camp is less time for prospects to prove they belong. The official camp roster features 50 players, but Blashill <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/09/13/blackhawks-coach-jeff-blashill-training-camp-swagger-patrick-kane-bowen-byram" target="_blank" >plans to divide</a> it into NHL and non-NHL groups right away.</p><p>Realistically, there are 24 healthy Hawks vying for 23 spots on the opening-night roster.</p><p>That includes 14 forwards: Patrick Kane, Frank Nazar, Anton Frondell, Roman Kantserov, Tyler Bertuzzi, Oliver Moore, Ryan Greene, Nick Lardis, Ryan Donato, Teuvo Teravainen, Cole Smith, Jordan Greenway, Landon Slaggert and Andrew Mangiapane.</p><p>That also includes eight defensemen — Bowen Byram, Alex Vlasic, Wyatt Kaiser, Ian Cole, Artyom Levshunov, Sam Rinzel, Kevin Korchinski and Ethan Del Mastro — and two goalies, Spencer Knight and Arvid Soderblom.</p><p>Forward prospect <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/09/11/blackhawks-aj-spellacy-prospect-camp-sacha-boisvert-marek-vanacker" target="_blank" >AJ Spellacy</a>, despite impressive showings in prospect showcase games Monday and Tuesday, will almost certainly start his first pro season in Rockford. The same is true for Sacha Boisvert.</p><p>Young goalie Drew Commesso probably won't have a chance to steal Soderblom's backup job yet, either. In-season performance will determine who gets call-up opportunities.</p><h3><b>Del Mastro in flux</b></h3><p>Del Mastro finally signed a two-year, one-way contract carrying a $950,000 salary-cap hit Wednesday, getting him in camp. The big, physical 23-year-old defenseman had been one of the last unsigned restricted free agents around the league.</p><p>His situation remains in flux, though. He showed promise in 24 NHL games in 2024-25, but he struggled in camp and in 19 NHL games last season. He enters this camp as, presumably, the eighth defenseman (below Korchinski).</p><p>Can Del Mastro impress enough to convince the Hawks to carry eight defensemen on their opening roster? If not, since he's no longer waivers-exempt, he'll likely end up on waivers at the end of camp, with the Hawks hoping to send him to Rockford. </p><p>If they decide to waive a forward instead, Mangiapane or Slaggert could be in jeopardy.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-7b0000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Ethan Del Mastro signed a contract Wednesday, but his roster spot remains unclear.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Michael Reaves/Getty Images</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Line combos</b></h3><p>That's enough about the roster edges. The middle of it matters more, and there are plenty of lineup construction questions needing answers.</p><p>Frondell and Nazar will definitely start at center, but who will the other two centers be? Kantserov, Moore, Donato and Greene are all possibilities.</p><p>Plus, which center will slot next to Kane on the first line? Who will play on the opposite wing? And what will the entire second line look like? The Hawks' forward depth chart is a puzzle with seemingly dozens of different possible combinations.</p><p>On defense, will either Byram or Cole shift to the right side — their "off" side as left-handed shots — to solve the Hawks' handedness imbalance? Levshunov and Rinzel are their only natural righties.</p><p>Who will team up with Byram on the top pair? If he moves to the right, Vlasic would be a logical candidate. And who will take on the challenging task of pairing with and mentoring Levshunov?</p><h3><b>League drama</b></h3><p>The Hawks' uncertainties pale in comparison to some teams' conundrums. The news cycle around the NHL in the coming weeks could be popcorn-worthy.</p><p>In Winnipeg, franchise goalie Connor Hellebuyck has demanded a trade and reportedly won't report to Jets camp. His departure could open the Hawks' door to climbing up the Central Division slightly wider.</p><p>In Columbus and Carolina, young studs Adam Fantilli and Alexander Nikishin, respectively, remain unsigned RFAs. Fantilli and the Blue Jackets' asking prices reportedly aren't close, which is interesting considering Bedard and Ducks center Leo Carlsson — the other two members of the 2023 draft class' famed top three — sorted out their contracts months ago.</p><p>And in Detroit, franchise center Dylan Larkin has demanded a trade, been stripped of the captaincy and won't be at Red Wings camp, supposedly due to injury. The Wings' general manager situation seems messy, too, even with Shawn Horcoff now given an interim tag.</p>

entries.title: Swashbuckling ‘The Princess Bride’ musical will stage pre-Broadway tryout in Chicago next July
entries.summary: <p>The anticipated new Broadway musical “The Princess Bride” is swashbuckling its way to Chicago, with a premiere at the James M. Nederlander Theatre next July.</p><p>The highly anticipated remake of William Goldman’s novel and the 1980s fantasy film by Rob Reiner promises to maintain the sword fighting and romance from the past with a fresh cast and an all-star creative team.</p><p>“The Princess Bride" is aiming to be Broadway’s next must-see musical, with a book by Tony Award winner Bob Martin (“The Drowsy Chaperone”) and Tony nominee Rick Elice (“Jersey Boys”), music and lyrics by Oscar-winning composers Kristen Anderson-Lopez (“Frozen”) and EGOT winner Robert Lopez (“Frozen,” “The Book of Mormon”), direction by Tony entries.title: Sputtering White Sox fall out of AL Central lead for the first time since July 4
entries.summary: <p>CLEVELAND — Pictures of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/14/tristan-peters-18-pitch-walk-baserunning-play-and-dumb-stuff-key-crucial-win-in-cleveland-sam-antonacci-sean-burke-will-venable-chris-getz-cleveland-guadians-white-sox" >happier moments from the season</a> hung up along the tunnel to the visitors’ dugout, a loud thud of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/15/white-sox-with-moments-to-second-guess-after-crushing-walk-off-loss-in-cleveland-sam-antonacci-grant-taylor-brayan-rocchio-will-venable-kyle-teel-davis-martin" target="_blank" ><u>someone taking out their frustration on a wall after Tuesday night’s walk-off loss</u></a>, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/16/tommy-pham-activated-munetaka-murakami-benched-for-all-important-series-finale-in-cleveland-will-venable-chris-getz-drew-thorpe-edgar-quero" target="_blank" ><u>Tommy Pham accelerating his return from the injured list</u></a> with a literal elevator pitch to general manager Chris Getz.</p><p>The issue is not these individual actions, but the wounds in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> playoff pursuits to which they’re responding, which remained on display in a 6-3 loss at Progressive Field that knocked them out of first place — by a half-game — in the American League Central for the first time since Independence Day.</p><p>“A tough series; I think that's a good characterization of that one,” said manager Will Venable.</p><p>Pham was signed simply to hit left-handed pitching, which the 38-year-old proved he can still provide with a thunderous, go-ahead three-run blast off Guardians ace Parker Messick in the fifth inning on Wednesday. The larger problem is that the Sox lineup has ached for right-handed balance because Munetaka Murakami and Colson Montgomery have ceased being everyday middle-of-the-order forces in the second half.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Tommy Pham turns the tide with a HUGE 3-run homer 💪 <a href="https://t.co/5MRpw9vt4b">pic.twitter.com/5MRpw9vt4b</a></p>— MLB (@MLB) <a href="https://x.com/MLB/status/2100291129870614769?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 16, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>“We ended up losing, man, so it's pointless,” Pham said of his homer.</p><p>Expressions of postgame frustration are natural, and the cost of playing games in September that matter deeply. The larger problem is even for an overhauled White Sox team, it’s become familiar in the ballpark, where the fourth-worst offense in MLB has walked off the Sox three times this year, before rallying for four sixth-inning runs — all with two outs — off Sean Newcomb; <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/31/white-sox-sean-newcomb-starter-or-reliever-bullpen-will-venable-grant-taylor-sean-burke-free-agency-chris-getz-rotation-relief" target="_blank" ><u>a rock of the team’s bullpen all year long</u></a>.</p><p>“I haven’t been myself,” said Newcomb, scored upon in five of his last six outings. “Just not being super crisp, hitters being more in tune with what I’m doing. It’s just part of it. There’s ups and downs throughout the season, it just sucks it’s coming now.”</p><p>As promised, Venable managed his pitchers with playoff intensity, dancing on the border between proactive, and overcooking it. In the wake of four-straight poor starts, Anthony Kay had anticipated getting pulled before facing Cleveland’s lineup a third time, even with his velocity up and the two runs he allowed in four innings being unearned due to a freak Chase Meidroth error was the ball was knocked out of his glove on a tag.</p><p>But the shorter start had Venable pursuing a second inning from Hagen Smith, who threw two innings in the series opener. So, the Sox manager blamed himself for the two walks Smith issued that Newcomb couldn’t clean up.</p><p>Facilitating a relaxed atmosphere is one of Will Venable’s central accomplishments. The larger problem beyond the photos, or reports of another jovial pregame hitters meeting on Wednesday, is they’re aimed at restoring a looseness that’s been evaporating whenever the White Sox have runners in scoring position.</p><p>After a 1-for-8 showing on Wednesday, the Sox are 14-for-72 with runners in scoring position (.194) over their last nine games, and 3-for-14 with the bases loaded. The one hit came from Pham.</p><p>“It's a team sport, but also a lot of stuff is individual,” Pham said of the RISP struggles. “Everybody has to look at themselves individually, and evaluate.”</p><p>If the White Sox evaluate, they have 10 games left, are even with division-leading Cleveland in the loss column, and are in possession of a tiebreaker and a relatively soft closing schedule.</p><p>They also have a high-power, low-contact offense that’s tilting toward the latter trait in crucial moments, their heavily-used bullpen cornerstones are faltering, and are depending on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/15/a-new-and-improved-david-sandlin-should-have-staying-power-in-white-sox-rotation-noah-schultz-colson-montgomery-will-venable-brian-bannister-jose-urquidy" target="_blank" ><u>rookie David Sandlin in the rotation this week</u></a>, because trade deadline headliner Luis Castillo has pitched his way out of their immediate plans.</p><p>As vital as this series in Cleveland was, what lies ahead is now even more crucial.</p><p>“We knew that this series wasn't going to define how the end of this year goes for us,” Venable said. “Tough to not have that lead, but at the same time, we’ve got a long ways to go here. A lot can happen.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/16/tommy-pham-activated-munetaka-murakami-benched-for-all-important-series-finale-in-cleveland-will-venable-chris-getz-drew-thorpe-edgar-quero" >Tommy Pham talks his way off IL, belts a homer, but can’t stop White Sox slide in Cleveland</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Judy Markey, beloved co-host of the "Kathy and Judy Show," dies at 82
entries.summary: <p></p><p></p><p></p><p>Chicago radio personality Judy Markey was never embarrassed to be real on air, whether sharing a personal story or pointing at something silly she'd done. </p><p>Like the time she drove away from a gas station with the pump still in her gas tank.</p><p>Sharing such tales with charm and ease was part of the magic she brought to the "Kathy and Judy Show" alongside her co-host and close friend Kathy O'Malley.</p><p>The groundbreaking show became the first in Chicago radio history hosted by women in a heavily male-dominated industry. It allowed a largely female audience to be seen and heard over shared joys and struggles — mundane and extraordinary — in a sisterhood of sorts known as “The Girlfriends.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Judy Markey (left) and Kathy O’Malley at their WGN-720 studio in 1995.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Nancy Stuenkel/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>A good number of male listeners also considered themselves part of the group. </p><p>Their weekday show aired on WGN-AM (720) from 1989 to 2009 and was picked up again in 2013 for a four-year run on weekends.</p><p>Ms. Markey, who suffered a degenerative neurological disorder, died Friday in Switzerland, where she chose a voluntary assisted death.</p><p>She was 82 and had no fear in her last months and moments, said her husband, Tom Collinger.</p><p>Before passing, she had a couple bites of a Snickers and said she had a headache.</p><p>"I said 'Do you want some Advil? And she said 'I kind of want something a little stronger,'" recalled Collinger, noting that her last joke landed with everyone in the room.</p><p>"She had a life that exceeded all her expectations. In the end she was comforting others," said Collinger, a professor emeritus at Northwestern University.</p><p>The "Kathy and Judy Show" was marked by genuine, relatable silliness and laughter. It included segments like "Sex Thursday" where listeners would share personal experiences.</p><p>Ms. Markey created an anonymous method for people to call in and share intimate things. Men were called "Vince," and women were called "Rhonda."</p><p>During their "Speak your Piece" segment, listeners called to vent and share whatever was on their minds.</p><p>There was the annual "Merry Medical Christmas Letters" in which the duo read family newsletters submitted by listeners that, instead of updates on vacations and newborns, were hilariously filled with TMI level details of surgeries, medical diagnoses and bodily ailments of the past year.</p><p>One radio moment that still makes fans smile occurred when Ms. Markey shared her annoyance that a new dishwasher delivered to her house came with a hideous turquoise trim. After some "They didn't!" and "They did!" the listener calls began pouring in, and it was quickly established that the turquoise was actually just plastic covering to protect the finish that could be peeled off.</p><p>Ms. Markey was incredulous at first. It made for great radio.</p><p>The show could just as easily veer toward serious topics, like the time around the turn of the century when a conservative group declared all women who had abortions suffered mental health issues afterward.</p><p>"We didn't feel that was entirely accurate," O'Malley recalled on WGN-AM following Ms. Markey's death. "And we asked for women to call who had had an abortion and to say whether or not that was true for them, and the first person to say 'I have had an abortion' was Judy Markey, which I thought was remarkably brave and powerful, and she opened the floodgates. The lines lit up with women who said 'I have had an abortion and I'm OK' and 'I have had an abortion and I haven't sunk into depression' ... we couldn't take all the calls. It was really remarkable."</p><p>She and Ms. Markey spoke about things others might shy away from, "but why not talk about them because they were real life, and that was as much Judy as the wacky stuff," O'Malley told the Sun-Times.</p><p>"We were not bull----. We said things that were true and things other people didn't want to say," O'Malley said. "I loved her so much. She was something else."</p><p>The show was immensely popular. The duo held annual fan conventions at the Hilton Hotel on Michigan Avenue.</p><p>A poem O'Malley posted on social media after the show went off the air for good drew more than 166,000 likes in just five days, according to former Sun-Times media columnist Robert Feder.</p><p>"Our listeners were the best part of our show," O'Malley said.</p><p>Ms. Markey was born Feb. 18, 1944, in Cleveland to Johnny and Lois Lindheim. Her parents ran a record store and a dance hall before moving to Beverly Hills, Calif., when Ms. Markey was 13.</p><p>Ms. Markey studied journalism at Northwestern and worked in administrative positions for an advertising agency and a book publisher in New York before she married her first husband, Tom Markey. She traveled with him to Europe, where the couple lived in several countries as her husband worked as an executive with Abbott Labs.</p><p>When the couple returned to the Chicago area, Ms. Markey had two small children and dreams of a new career. They later divorced.</p><p>"I remember we were driving in a snowstorm in Wilmette, and I told her I wanted to be an interior designer and she told me she wanted to be a writer," recalled her good friend Chris Paschen.</p><p>Ms. Markey successfully pitched a few ideas to magazines like Cosmopolitan and Glamour and gained momentum as a writer. She then started a steady gig writing slice-of-life columns for the Sun-Times. Meanwhile, O'Malley was working as a columnist at the Chicago Tribune.</p><p>Ms. Markey and O'Malley met in the '80s when the now-dissolved Chicago City Ballet cast media personalities to play the wicked stepmother in their Thanksgiving productions of "Cinderella." Each had a turn in the role. They met during rehearsals and hit it off immediately.</p><p>Each had also served as an occasional guest on WGN radio programs.</p><p>In 1989, WGN’s program director Lorna Gladstone thought their combined viewpoints and wit could make something special on the radio. Gladstone teamed them on air for the first time in a low-stakes test run during a time slot that overlapped the Super Bowl.</p><p>Their foot was in the door. They kicked it open.</p><p>It was a coincidence that Ms. Markey died a day before Illinois’ new “medical aid in dying” law went into effect, allowing terminally ill adults to seek life-ending medication from doctors.</p><p>Ms. Markey, who split time between Highland Park and Tucson in recent years, hoped her death would add to and broaden the conversation surrounding a person's right to choose to die, her husband said.</p><p>In addition to her husband, Ms. Markey is survived by her daughter, Erin Markey; son Adam Markey; stepson Zach Collinger; stepdaughter Kate Collinger Buxton; son-in-law Pat Buxton; and two grandchildren.</p><p>A private celebration of life will be held Thursday. It will be live-streamed at 11 a.m., preceded by a short video at 10:45 a.m. A link to the live stream can be found at <a class="Link" href="http://everloved.com" target="_blank" >everloved.com</a>, as well as below:</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/aT1mjkfYQQc?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Celebration of Judy Markey"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p>
